content.text: Welcome to the UK Cultural Orientation (UKCO) App.

This app has been designed to help you prepare for life in the United Kingdom. Whether you are preparing to travel or have already arrived, the information in this app will help you feel more confident and informed.
The app covers 10 topics to help you settle into life in the UK:

items: Your First Few Weeks in the UK

content.text: Each topic includes key information, helpful tips and a short quiz to test your understanding.
The United Kingdom (UK) is made up of four countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The UK is an island nation located off the northwestern coast of Europe.
The UK mainland is about 870 miles (1,400 km) from north to south. The population is approximately 67.6 million people.

content.title: Each country has its own capital city:

content.text: Other major cities include Manchester, Birmingham, Liverpool, Leeds, Bristol, Glasgow, Aberdeen, Swansea and Newport.
English is the main language spoken in the UK. However, there are also regional languages:

items: Gaelic is spoken in parts of Scotland
Irish Gaelic is spoken in parts of Northern Ireland

content.text: You will hear many different accents and dialects across the UK. Learning English is essential for settling into life in the UK.
The UK has a temperate climate with rainfall throughout the year. Temperatures rarely drop below -11°C or rise above 35°C.

content.title: Seasons in the UK:
items: Spring (March - May): Often rainy, with flowers and trees blooming.
Summer (June - August): The warmest season with long sunny days and occasional thunderstorms.
Autumn (September - November): Days get colder, leaves fall from trees, and it can be wet and windy.
Winter (December - February): The coldest season with freezing temperatures, ice and sometimes snow.

content.text: Clocks go forward one hour in March and back one hour in October for daylight savings.
The UK has several public holidays (called Bank Holidays) when banks and many businesses are closed.
The UK is a constitutional monarchy and a parliamentary democracy.
Head of State: King Charles III. Prime Minister: Sir Keir Starmer.
Parliament has three parts: the King, the House of Lords and the House of Commons.
The official religion is Christianity, but the UK is a multi-faith society. You are free to practise your religion.

content.text: Your journey to the UK will be arranged by staff from the International Organization for Migration (IOM). IOM staff will guide you through every step of the travel process.
You should think carefully about what to pack. Prioritise essential belongings and items with personal value.
Do bring:

items: Warm clothes for UK weather (coat, hat, scarf, gloves)
Important documents (kept in your hand luggage)
Prescription medication and a doctor’s letter explaining what it is
Items with sentimental value (photos, small keepsakes)
Baby supplies if needed (nappies, formula, bottles, change of clothes)

content.text: Do NOT pack:

items: Knives, scissors, sharp objects or weapons
Large amounts of cash without declaring it

content.text: Each passenger is usually allowed one or two checked bags (approximately 23kg each) and one carry-on bag.

When you arrive in the UK, you will go through UK immigration (border control). You will need to show your travel documents from the IOM bag.
Immigration officers may ask you questions. Answer calmly and honestly.
After passing through immigration, collect your checked luggage from the baggage claim area.
Someone will be waiting to meet you after you collect your luggage. They will take you to your accommodation.

units.title: YOUR FIRST FEW WEEKS IN THE UK

sections.title: Your Legal Status in the UK

content.text: When you arrive in the UK, you will have the legal right to stay. This means that:

items: You can access public services such as healthcare and schools
You have the right to work and can look for work as soon as you arrive
You can apply for benefits (financial support from the government) to cover your basic living costs until you find work
You can apply for British citizenship in the future under existing rules

content.text: After you arrive in the UK, you will be supported to access your eVisa. This is done through an online UKVI (UK Visas and Immigration) account, which will be set up for you by the UK Home Office. Every member of your family receives an eVisa, including children and babies. Your eVisa is free of charge.
Your eVisa is very important. It is evidence of your identity and legal status in the UK. You will need your eVisa to access benefits, the NHS (National Health Service) and other services.
Unlike a physical document, an eVisa cannot be lost, damaged or stolen. You must keep access to your UKVI account safe and secure.
When you arrive in the UK, you will have support to help you settle in. Someone will meet you at the airport and take you to your accommodation. You will not have to pay for transport.
If your flight arrives late in the evening, you may be accommodated overnight, and food and drinks will be provided.
Your support network will help you to:

items: Register children and teenagers at local schools or college
Register adults at English language and literacy classes
Register with a local GP (doctor) and dentist
Understand UK money and how to budget
Find places to shop, places of worship, schools, parks and public transport
Access mental health services if needed
Apply for jobs (though they cannot give you a job directly)

content.text: The people supporting you will not be available at all times. You will need to start managing some things on your own.
During working hours (Monday to Friday), your support contacts will be available to help. Outside of these hours, you may need to handle some things yourself.
It is important to:

items: Ask questions whenever you are unsure about something
Tell your support contacts if you have any concerns or worries
Start learning English as soon as possible - this is the most important step towards independence

content.text: There are extensive train, bus and tram services across the UK. Public transport is safe and used by everyone, regardless of age and gender.
Taxis are available but more expensive. Many people use apps like Uber or Bolt to book a ride.
Your support network will help you understand local public transport. Tips for saving money:

items: Take a bus rather than a train
Buy a weekly or monthly ticket instead of individual tickets
Use a pre-paid card or contactless bank card to pay

content.text: You must always pay for a ticket for your entire journey. If you do not, you could receive a fine.
Cycling is a popular and affordable way to get around. In some areas, you can hire bikes.
If you cycle, remember:

items: Wear a cycle helmet that fits correctly
Wear bright or reflective clothing so others can see you
Use cycle lanes and cycle tracks where available

content.text: To drive a car in the UK, you must have:

text: A fully registered car with a valid MOT and up-to-date vehicle tax

content.text: Important rules:

items: All passengers must wear seat belts
Children must travel in the correct child safety seat
It is a criminal offence to use your mobile phone while driving
Driving without a licence, insurance, or proper vehicle tax is a criminal offence

content.text: You can drive on your existing licence for 12 months. After that, you must pass UK theory and practical tests (in English only; voiceover available for reading difficulties).
Buying and insuring a car is expensive. Public transport is often cheaper.
The UK is a multi-faith society. There are mosques, churches, synagogues, temples and other places of worship.
Your support network will help you find local places of worship. If there is none for your faith nearby, they can help you find a community prayer space and a faith leader.
Many resettled people have found support, friendship and community through their place of worship.
Learning and speaking English is key to integration and will help you:
The British Council offers free tools:
Your support network will help you register for local English classes.
Education for children is free and compulsory in the UK:

items: England, Wales and Scotland: ages 5 to 16
England: ages 16 to 18 must continue in education or training

content.text: After 16, options include college, vocational courses, apprenticeships and university.
You are responsible for ensuring your children attend school every day. Not doing so can result in a fine.
In Scotland, university tuition is free (subject to entry requirements). Elsewhere, student loans are available.

sections.title: Can My Family Join Me in the UK?

content.text: If you have been resettled without some family members, it is important to understand:

items: Resettlement places are very limited globally. The likelihood of additional family members being identified is unfortunately very low.
UK Family Reunion rules allow spouses (if married before arrival) and dependent children under 18 to apply. In exceptional circumstances, others may qualify.
There is no guarantee that other family members will be able to join you.

content.text: If you find it difficult to be separated from your family, please speak with your support network for help.
If family members outside the UK have safety concerns, they should contact their nearest UNHCR office.
